query: W melts near 3422 °C, whereas Cu boils near 2562 °C, so conventional induction or arc-plasma casting cannot readily yield a uniform W–Cu material. Phase separation and void formation can impair thermal transport. Filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder can leave defects; spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can produce finer, more uniform structures but can also leave voids; vapor-coated W powders have been sintered to achieve near-perfect contact between the constituents; and metal 3D printing has also been explored. Starting from W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix for heat transfer under irradiation in fusion-reactor joints, what single intervention could overcome these limitations while preserving mechanical durability? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts an outcome relative to a named existing fabrication baseline, defines the processing and service boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment and observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A single pulsed compression plasma flow (CPF) treatment applied to pre-deposited copper coatings on tungsten particles embedded in a copper matrix will produce an ultrafine, void‐free interfacial mixing (including partial W(Cu) solid solution formation) that enhances thermal transport and irradiation durability compared to composites fabricated by conventional spark‐plasma sintering or vapor‐coating and sintering alone.
generation.material_initial_state: W particles or connected W structures within a Cu matrix, where tungsten surfaces have been uniformly pre-coated with a thin layer of copper (e.g., via vapor deposition).
generation.intervention: Subject the composite to a pulsed compression plasma flow treatment with a controlled absorbed energy density (approximately 35–55 J/cm²) and short pulse durations (~100 μs) to rapidly melt and mix the copper coating with the near-surface tungsten.
generation.conditions: Processing to be performed in a controlled atmosphere (e.g., nitrogen plasma) to avoid unwanted nitride formation, with pulse parameters optimized for rapid heating and cooling (rates of 10^6–10^7 K/s). Service conditions are under high heat flux and irradiation typical of fusion reactor joints.
generation.structural_mediator: The rapid, localized melting and subsequent ultrafast quenching leads to the formation of a finely intermixed interface with a distorted tungsten lattice (W(Cu) solid solution) that suppresses void formation and phase separation.
generation.mechanism: The CPF generates a locally superheated surface layer that facilitates liquid-phase mixing between copper and tungsten at the interfacial region. Upon rapid quenching, the high cooling rate traps copper atoms into the tungsten lattice, forming a metastable, defect-rich solid solution that minimizes interfacial voids and improves adhesion and thermal conductivity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline fabricated by vapor-coated tungsten powders sintered by conventional methods, the CPF-treated composite will exhibit reduced void density, enhanced thermal diffusivity, and improved radiation resistance while preserving mechanical durability.
generation.baseline: Vapor-coated tungsten powders assembled into a Cu matrix and sintered to achieve near-perfect contact, which often still suffers from residual defects and limited interfacial mixing.
generation.boundary: Processing is limited to conditions where the CPF pulse parameters can achieve complete surface melting without excessive copper evaporation (below energies that would induce overheating), and the composite must be used in fusion-reactor joint applications with high thermal flux and neutron/ion irradiation but at temperatures below the degradation thresholds of the metastable interfacial phases.
generation.uncertainty: The exact pulse energy and cooling rate window that yields the ideal W(Cu) solid solution without copper loss (as indicated in PMC11433029 sections 3.1 and 4) are not fully defined. It is also uncertain how slight variations in the copper pre-coating thickness influence the formation of void-free interfaces.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of W–Cu composites: one with copper pre-coated on tungsten particles and subjected to CPF treatment (using the stated pulse parameters) and one processed by vapor coating and conventional sintering. Assess microstructural features via high-resolution TEM and SEM along with positron annihilation techniques for vacancy/void analysis. Perform thermal diffusivity measurements (e.g., using laser flash analysis) and irradiation tests simulating fusion reactor conditions.
measurements: Void density and interfacial continuity (via electron microscopy)
Phase identification and lattice parameter shifts (using XRD)
Thermal diffusivity values pre- and post-irradiation
Mechanical durability via microhardness and tensile testing under simulated irradiation conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the CPF-treated samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in interfacial void density, no measurable formation of a mixed W(Cu) phase, or if their thermal transport or radiation resistance properties are not superior (or are inferior) to those of the conventional vapor-coated, sintered baseline.

cited_evidence.text: Indeed, a crucial result of the pulsed treatment of the metal surfaces is a quenching effect due to the high solidification rate. When the heat transfer from the plasma stream stops, cooling of the melted layers occurs. Because of a strong correlation between the thickness of the non-molten metal part and the molten surface layer, the cooling rate can reach 106–107 K/s [,,]. The quenching effect produces an excess concentration of vacancies, which can decrease the lattice parameters of the crystal structure in the modified metals. However, the results of the effect of plasma with the same energies on pure tungsten, without any other metal as a coating, showed constant values of its lattice parameters []. Thus, it can be assumed that the presence of copper atoms in the crystal lattice of tungsten results in solid solution W(Cu) formation. The atomic radius of copper (128 pm) is less than that of tungsten (141 pm), and the formation of W(Cu) solid solution can be associated with its lattice parameter decrease. Overall, the work demonstrated the fundamental opportunity of creating alloys based on tungsten and copper by successively applying copper coating to the tungsten surface and using pulsed action of compression plasma flows with a pulse duration of 100 μs, with an absorbed energy density of 35–55 J/cm2. The results demonstrate the formation of a composite structure based on individual phases of tungsten and copper, and due to the high-speed crystallization of the molten surface layer, a solid solution of W(Cu) with a distorted crystal lattice is formed. Analysis of radiation effects during irradiation of tungsten and tungsten-copper alloy samples with helium ions with an energy of 40 keV and doses of (1–3) × 1017 cm−2 showed that tungsten samples pre-treated with CPF in the melting and mixing mode of the near-surface layer have increased radiation resistance. In the near-surface region, corresponding to the helium ion range, there is a distortion of the tungsten phase crystal lattice, which causes mechanical destruction of the surface.
